name: Fedor and coupons
description: All our characters have hobbies. The same is true for Fedor. He enjoys shopping in the neighboring supermarket. The goods in the supermarket have unique integer ids. Also, for every integer there is a product with id equal to this integer. Fedor has n discount coupons, the i -th of them can be used with products with ids ranging from l i to r i , inclusive. Today Fedor wants to take exactly k coupons with him. Fedor wants to choose the k coupons in such a way that the number of such products x that all coupons can be used with this product x is as large as possible (for better understanding, see examples). Fedor wants to save his time as well, so he asks you to choose coupons for him. Help Fedor!
input_specification: The first line contains two integers n and k ( 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 3·10 5 ) — the number of coupons Fedor has, and the number of coupons he wants to choose. Each of the next n lines contains two integers l i and r i ( - 10 9 ≤ l i ≤ r i ≤ 10 9 ) — the description of the i -th coupon. The coupons can be equal.
output_specification: In the first line print single integer — the maximum number of products with which all the chosen coupons can be used. The products with which at least one coupon cannot be used shouldn't be counted. In the second line print k distinct integers p 1 , p 2 , ..., p k ( 1 ≤ p i ≤ n ) — the ids of the coupons which Fedor should choose. If there are multiple answers, print any of them.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 754D — Fedor and coupons [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
